日本が直面している最も深刻な課題の一つが少子高齢化である。出生率の低下が続く一方で、平均寿命は世界でも有数の長さを保っている。その結果、働く世代が支えるべき高齢者の割合は年々高まり、年金や医療保険の制度は大きな負担を強いられている。政府は保育施設の拡充や育児休業制度の整備を進めてきたが、出生率の回復には至っていない。問題の根はむしろ、長時間労働や住宅費の高さといった、子育てを選びにくくする社会構造そのものにあるという指摘も根強い。

One of the most serious challenges facing Japan is its declining birth rate and ageing population. While the birth rate continues to fall, average life expectancy remains among the longest in the world. As a result the proportion of elderly people that the working generation must support rises year by year, and the pension and health insurance systems are placed under great strain. The government has expanded childcare facilities and developed parental leave systems, but this has not led to a recovery in the birth rate. There is a persistent argument that the root of the problem lies rather in the social structure itself — long working hours and high housing costs — which makes choosing to raise children difficult.

テレビやインターネットの普及により、日本各地の方言は急速に失われつつあると言われてきた。確かに、若い世代ほど共通語に近い話し方をする傾向は強い。しかし近年は、方言をあえて用いることで親しみを表現したり、地域の個性を示したりする動きも見られる。方言は単なる古い言葉の残りではなく、その土地の人間関係や価値観を映す鏡でもある。標準化が進むほど、失われるものの大きさに気づかされるのかもしれない。

It has been said that with the spread of television and the internet, regional dialects across Japan are rapidly being lost. It is true that the younger the generation, the stronger the tendency to speak in a way close to standard Japanese. In recent years, however, there has also been a movement to use dialect deliberately to express familiarity or to show regional character. Dialect is not merely the remains of old speech but a mirror reflecting the human relationships and values of a place. Perhaps the further standardisation goes, the more we are made aware of the scale of what is lost.
